analysis.one_liner: Adds layers of analysis, review, and litigation-friendly rules before federal agencies can issue major regulations.
analysis.headline: The Senate bill was referred to the Homeland Security Committee on May 12, 2025 and has had no hearing, vote, or further action since.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill rewrites the rulemaking process every federal agency must follow. Agencies would have to study at least three alternatives to any major rule, open a public docket before proposing it, wait longer for comments, and — as the default — adopt the alternative that costs regulated businesses the least, unless a White House budget-office official signs off otherwise. It would also let courts re-decide legal questions agencies settled and make it easier to challenge agency guidance. Rules already issued would not be affected.
analysis.who_benefits: Companies subject to federal regulation — banks, energy producers, manufacturers, drug makers, and others — would gain, because major rules would take longer, cost less to them by default, and be easier to overturn in court. Business groups have long backed similar versions of this bill for that reason.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Regulated industries and their litigation challenges

how_it_helps.text: For any 'major rule' — one affecting the economy by $100 million or more, raising costs or prices significantly, or raising novel legal issues — the agency must adopt the alternative that maximizes net benefits and, by default, the least costly option, unless the OIRA Administrator approves otherwise [S2].

Before proposing a major rule, an agency must publish an advance notice at least 90 days early, open a public docket, put every study and model it relied on into that docket, and allow a 90-day comment period plus a 30-day window for commenters to respond to each other [S2].
All communications between an agency and stakeholders who could benefit from a proposed rule must be published in the Federal Register with the proposal [S2].
Courts reviewing rules would decide questions of law 'de novo' — fresh, without deferring to the agency's reading — and could remand a rule to the agency without striking it down [S2].
Every major rule would get a published framework for measuring whether it worked, and periodic assessments of whether it should be modified or repealed [S2].

analysis.who_pays: If passed, ordinary people would bear the cost through slower and, in the default case, weaker federal protections — clean air and water rules, workplace safety standards, food and drug safety, and consumer financial rules all move through this process. Federal agencies would also spend much more time on paperwork for each rule.
analysis.who_pays_short: Everyone who relies on federal protections

drawbacks.text: The default requirement to adopt the least-costly alternative for major rules would push agencies toward weaker protections for public health, safety, and the environment, since a cheaper rule for industry is often a weaker rule for the public [S2].
The added advance notice, docket, cost-benefit, and comment requirements would stretch an already multi-year rulemaking process further, delaying protections even when a rule is urgent [S2].

Requiring de novo court review of legal questions and precluding judicial review of the OIRA Administrator's decisions would shift power from expert agencies to courts and to a single White House political appointee [S2].

Supporters counter that the bill increases transparency — public dockets, plain-language summaries, published back-channel contacts — and forces agencies to justify rules with real cost-benefit analysis rather than assume a rule is good because it is protective [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The transparency pieces — open dockets, published ex parte contacts, plain-language summaries — have real value, and a few of them codify practices agencies already follow. But the bill's centerpiece, the least-costly default for major rules plus easier court challenges, is the part that would most change outcomes, and it runs in one direction: fewer, slower, and weaker protections for the public, and lower compliance costs for regulated firms. The bill does carve out emergencies and monetary policy, but those exceptions are narrow compared with the volume of rules that would flow through the new process.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee, where it has sat without a hearing or vote since May 2025.

narrative.text: Sen. James Lankford introduced the bill in the Senate on May 12, 2025 [S1][S4].
The same day, the Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs [S4].
It has one cosponsor, a Senate Republican, and no further recorded action since referral [S3][S4].
The bill text states it would not apply to any rulemaking already pending or completed when the Act is enacted, so existing rules would be untouched even if it passed [S2].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one yet — with the bill stalled in committee, agencies still operate under the current rulemaking process and no one has gained or lost.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: No one yet; the bill is stalled in committee

for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, the only cosponsor it has.

for.what_they_did: Business and industry coalitions have historically championed versions of the Regulatory Accountability Act, arguing agencies issue costly rules without adequate cost-benefit analysis; no recorded action on this bill appears in the sources.

sides.party_line_note: There has been no vote and no committee action, so no partisan breakdown exists; the bill's only recorded support so far is two Republicans with no Democratic cosponsors [S3].

industries.note: Major rules would default to the least-costly option for these firms and would face longer, more heavily documented processes, making protections like pollution limits or workplace standards weaker or slower [S2]. The industry's gain is the public's cost when a cheaper rule means a weaker one.

industries.industry: Companies and law firms challenging federal rules
industries.note: De novo court review of legal questions, remand without vacatur, and review of agency guidance would make lawsuits against rules more likely to succeed or at least to delay them [S2]. Litigation becomes a cheaper tool for delaying protections the public is waiting on.

Agencies would lose speed and discretion — advance notices, dockets, least-costly defaults, and retrospective assessments for every major rule — but the bill also directs agencies to publish the data behind their rules and respond to every significant comment, which serves the public as well [S2].

analysis.trajectory: Bills that sit in a Senate committee with a single cosponsor and no scheduled hearing usually die quietly when the Congress ends in January 2027. A similar Regulatory Accountability Act passed the House in 2017 under full Republican control, so a path exists if Senate leadership prioritizes it, but nothing in the record so far — no hearing, no committee vote, no floor action — suggests that is happening.
